Those who interpret the Qur'an have said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Musarrik ibn Aban narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from a man he did not name, from Abu al-Jawza', who said: I said to Ibn Abbas: "Who are those whom God began with woe?" He said: "They are those who go about spreading tale-bearing (namima), who separate loved ones, and who seek out the faults of others."

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from his father, from a man of Basra, from Abu al-Jawza', who said: I said to Ibn Abbas: "Who are those whom God summoned to woe?" Then he mentioned something similar to the report of Musarrik ibn Aban.

It has been transmitted from Mujahid a view opposite to this, namely:

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "The hamaza is the slanderer, and the lumaza is the one who eats the flesh of people."

It has also been transmitted from him a view contrary to these two, namely:

- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: Yahya narrated to us, he said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: he said: "One of them is the one who eats the flesh of people, and the other is the slanderer." This indicates that the one who transmitted this hadith had become confused about the interpretation of the two words, which is why the narrators' accounts from him differ as I have mentioned.

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: As for the hamaza, it is eating the flesh of people; and as for the lumaza, it is slandering them.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah, from Qatada, who said: "The hamaza is one who eats the flesh of people; the lumaza is one who slanders them."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Khuthaym, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: he said: "Woe to every slanderer who backbites."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliya, who said: "The hamaza: he scorns him to his face, and the lumaza: from behind his back."

Others have said on this matter:

- Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding the saying of God: ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: "The hamaza is one who scorns people with his hand and strikes them with his tongue, and the lumaza is one who mocks them with his tongue and disparages them."

There has been difference regarding His saying ﴿Woe to every scorner﴾. Some said: it refers to a specific idolater, and some who said this view said: he is Jamil ibn Amir al-Jumahi.

Others among them said: he is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.

Mention of those who said it refers to a specific idolater:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: he said: "An idolater who used to mock people and scorn them."

- Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu Asim narrated to us, he said: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from a man of al-Raqqa who said: "It was revealed concerning Jamil ibn Amir al-Jumahi."

- al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, regarding His saying ﴿scorner and mocker﴾: "It is not specific to anyone; it was revealed concerning all of the Banu Amir." Warqa' said: "al-Raqashi claimed it."

Some of the scholars of Arabic said: this is of the type where the Arabs mention a general name for a thing while intending a particular one, as when a man says to someone: "I will never visit you," and the other replies: "Everyone who does not visit me, then he is not a visitor," the speaker intending a reply to his companion who said to him: "I will never visit you."

Others said: rather, it is meant generally, for everyone who has this attribute, and no other particular intention is meant.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu Asim narrated to us, he said: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God: ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: "It is not specific to anyone."

The correct view on this matter is that it should be said: God has spoken generally of every scorner and mocker, everyone who has the attribute by which this described one was described, whose path is his path, whoever he may be among people.

* *

His saying: ﴿who has gathered wealth and counted it﴾

He says: the one who gathered wealth and counted its number, and did not spend it in the way of God, nor paid God's right in it, but gathered it, stored it up and kept it.

The readers differed in reading this. Abu Ja'far from the readers of Medina, and the majority of the readers of Kufa except Asim, read "jamma'a" (with emphasis). The majority of the readers of Medina and the Hijaz, except Abu Ja'far, and the majority of the readers of Basra, and Asim from Kufa, read "jama'a" (without emphasis). All of them agree on the emphasis of the dal in ﴿wa 'addadahu﴾ in the sense that I have mentioned in its interpretation. It has been reported from some of the early scholars, through an unsound chain, that he read: "jama'a malan wa 'adadahu" with a light dal, meaning: he gathered wealth and gathered his clan and his numbers. This is a reading I do not consider permissible to recite, since it contradicts the readings of the regions and departs from what the community has agreed upon.

As for His saying ﴿jama'a malan﴾, both the emphatic and the non-emphatic forms are correct in it, since they are two well-known readings in the regional readings, close in meaning; whichever of them the reader recites is correct.

* *

His saying: ﴿He thinks his wealth will make him immortal﴾

He says: he thinks that his wealth, which he gathered and counted, and which he withheld from spending, will make him immortal in this world, averting death from him. It has been said: "akhladahu" means "yukhlidahu" (will make him immortal), as one says of a man who engages in an action that is the cause of his destruction: "So-and-so has perished by God, so-and-so has been ruined by God," meaning that he is ruined by doing that deed, though he has not yet perished nor been destroyed; and like a man who commits a grave sin: "So-and-so has entered the Fire by God."

* *

His saying: ﴿Nay!﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: it is not as he supposed; his wealth does not make him immortal.

Then He informed, may His praise be exalted, that he will be destroyed and punished for his deeds and sins that he used to commit in this world, so He said: ﴿He will surely be thrown into the Crushing﴾. He says: he will surely be hurled into the Crushing on the Day of Resurrection. "Al-Hutama" is one of the names of the Fire, just as it is called Jahannam, Saqar and Laza. I think it was named so because it crushes everything cast into it, just as a greedy man is called "al-hutama." It is reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that he used to read it: "layunbadhanna fi al-Hutama," meaning: this scorner and mocker and his wealth, and so he made it dual for that reason.

* *

His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Crushing is?﴾

He says: and what made you aware, O Muhammad, of what the Crushing is? Then He informed him what it is, saying, may His praise be exalted: it is ﴿the Fire of God, kindled, which rises over the hearts﴾. He says: whose pain and blaze reach the hearts. "Al-Ittila'" (rising over) and "al-buluugh" (reaching) may have the same meaning; it is related from the Arabs by report: "When did our land rise (tala'at)?" and "my land rose (talaat)": meaning it reached.

* *

His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: indeed the Crushing whose description I have given will be closed down upon them, meaning upon these scorners and mockers. ﴿Mu'sada﴾ means: sealed shut. It is recited with both forms (hamz and without hamz), and both have been read.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Talq narrated to us, from Ibn Zuhayr, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿Mu'sada﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Ubayd ibn Asbat narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from Fudayl ibn Marzuq, from Ata', regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Ya'qub narrated to us, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, who said: "In the Fire there is a man in a ravine of its ravines calling for about a thousand years: 'O Hannan! O Hannan!' The Lord of Might says to Jibril: 'Bring out My servant from the Fire.' He comes to it and finds it sealed shut, so he returns and says: 'O Lord, indeed it is closed down upon them.' He says: 'O Jibril, open it and bring My servant out of the Fire.' He opens it, and he comes out like a shadow, and is cast upon the shore of Paradise until God causes hair, flesh and blood to grow for him."

- Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, he said: Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from Mudarris ibn Abd Allah, who said: I heard al-Dahhak ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Locked shut upon them."

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: i.e., sealed shut.

- Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut. The Arabs say: 'awsada al-bab': he closed the door."

* *

His saying: ﴿in extended columns﴾

The readers differed in reading this. The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra recited ﴿fi 'amad﴾ with a fatha on the ayn and the mim. The majority of the readers of Kufa recited "fi 'umud" with a damma on the ayn and the mim. Our view on this is that both are well-known readings, each recited by scholars among the readers, and both are sound dialects. The Arabs pluralize "'amud" (column) as "'umudan" and "'amadan," with both letters vowelled with damma and with fatha; and similarly they do with "ihab" (hide), pluralized as "uhuban" with damma on the alif and the ha', and "ahaban" with fatha on both; and likewise "qadm." Whichever of them the reader recites is correct.

The people of interpretation differed on the meaning of this. Some said: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them in extended columns﴾ means: sealed shut and closed over them; and so it is in the reading of Abdullah, as it has reached us.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Qatada, regarding the reading of Abdullah: "Indeed, it will be closed down upon them in extended columns."

Others said: rather, the meaning is: they will be made to enter into columns, then those columns will be extended over them with pillars.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿in extended columns﴾: he said: "He will make them enter into columns, and they will be extended over them with pillars, and there will be chains around their necks, and the doors will be sealed shut with them."

- Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding ﴿in columns﴾: "of iron, they being bound in them, and those columns are of fire that have been heated by the fire, so they are of fire, extended over them."

Others said: they are columns in which they are tortured.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada regarding ﴿in extended columns﴾: "We used to be told that they are columns with which they are tortured in the Fire." Bishr said: Yazid said: in the reading of Qatada: "'amadin."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada regarding ﴿in extended columns﴾: he said: "A pillar with which they are tortured in the Fire."

The most correct of the sayings on this matter is the saying of the one who said: its meaning is that they will be tortured with columns in the Fire; and God knows best how He tortures them with them. No report has reached us that establishes the manner of their torment with them, nor has He placed for us any indication by which we might grasp the nature of that, so there is no statement on it other than what we have said, which is sound to us; and God knows best.

End of the commentary on Surat al-Humaza.

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: it is not as he supposed; his wealth does not make him immortal.

Then He informed, may His praise be exalted, that he will be destroyed and punished for his deeds and sins that he used to commit in this world, so He said: ﴿He will surely be thrown into the Crushing﴾. He says: he will surely be hurled into the Crushing on the Day of Resurrection. "Al-Hutama" is one of the names of the Fire, just as it is called Jahannam, Saqar and Laza. I think it was named so because it crushes everything cast into it, just as a greedy man is called "al-hutama." It is reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that he used to read it: "layunbadhanna fi al-Hutama," meaning: this scorner and mocker and his wealth, and so he made it dual for that reason.

* *

His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Crushing is?﴾

He says: and what made you aware, O Muhammad, of what the Crushing is? Then He informed him what it is, saying, may His praise be exalted: it is ﴿the Fire of God, kindled, which rises over the hearts﴾. He says: whose pain and blaze reach the hearts. "Al-Ittila'" (rising over) and "al-buluugh" (reaching) may have the same meaning; it is related from the Arabs by report: "When did our land rise (tala'at)?" and "my land rose (talaat)": meaning it reached.

* *

His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: indeed the Crushing whose description I have given will be closed down upon them, meaning upon these scorners and mockers. ﴿Mu'sada﴾ means: sealed shut. It is recited with both forms (hamz and without hamz), and both have been read.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Talq narrated to us, from Ibn Zuhayr, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿Mu'sada﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Ubayd ibn Asbat narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from Fudayl ibn Marzuq, from Ata', regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Ya'qub narrated to us, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, who said: "In the Fire there is a man in a ravine of its ravines calling for about a thousand years: 'O Hannan! O Hannan!' The Lord of Might says to Jibril: 'Bring out My servant from the Fire.' He comes to it and finds it sealed shut, so he returns and says: 'O Lord, indeed it is closed down upon them.' He says: 'O Jibril, open it and bring My servant out of the Fire.' He opens it, and he comes out like a shadow, and is cast upon the shore of Paradise until God causes hair, flesh and blood to grow for him."

- Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, he said: Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from Mudarris ibn Abd Allah, who said: I heard al-Dahhak ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Locked shut upon them."

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: i.e., sealed shut.

His saying: ﴿in extended columns﴾

Our view on this is that both are well-known readings, each recited by scholars among the readers, and both are sound dialects. The Arabs pluralize "'amud" (column) as "'umudan" and "'amadan," with both letters vowelled with damma and with fatha; and similarly they do with "ihab" (hide), pluralized as "uhuban" with damma on the alif and the ha', and "ahaban" with fatha on both; and likewise "qadm." Whichever of them the reader recites is correct.

It has been transmitted from Mujahid a view opposite to this, namely:

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "The hamaza is the slanderer, and the lumaza is the one who eats the flesh of people."

- Musarrik ibn Aban al-Hatstab narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, he said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

It has also been transmitted from him a view contrary to these two, namely:

- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: Yahya narrated to us, he said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: he said: "One of them is the one who eats the flesh of people, and the other is the slanderer." This indicates that the one who transmitted this hadith had become confused about the interpretation of the two words, which is why the narrators' accounts from him differ as I have mentioned.

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: As for the hamaza, it is eating the flesh of people; and as for the lumaza, it is slandering them.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah, from Qatada, who said: "The hamaza is one who eats the flesh of people; the lumaza is one who slanders them."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Khuthaym, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: he said: "Woe to every slanderer who backbites."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliya, who said: "The hamaza: he scorns him to his face, and the lumaza: from behind his back."

- Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, who said: "He scorns him and mocks him with his tongue and his eye, eats the flesh of people, and slanders them."

- al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "The hamaza is with the hand, and the lumaza is with the tongue."

Others have said on this matter:

- Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding the saying of God: ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: "The hamaza is one who scorns people with his hand and strikes them with his tongue, and the lumaza is one who mocks them with his tongue and disparages them."

There has been difference regarding His saying ﴿Woe to every scorner﴾. Some said: it refers to a specific idolater, and some who said this view said: he is Jamil ibn Amir al-Jumahi.

Others among them said: he is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.

Mention of those who said it refers to a specific idolater:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: he said: "An idolater who used to mock people and scorn them."

- Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu Asim narrated to us, he said: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from a man of al-Raqqa who said: "It was revealed concerning Jamil ibn Amir al-Jumahi."

- al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, regarding His saying ﴿scorner and mocker﴾: "It is not specific to anyone; it was revealed concerning all of the Banu Amir." Warqa' said: "al-Raqashi claimed it."

Some of the scholars of Arabic said: this is of the type where the Arabs mention a general name for a thing while intending a particular one, as when a man says to someone: "I will never visit you," and the other replies: "Everyone who does not visit me, then he is not a visitor," the speaker intending a reply to his companion who said to him: "I will never visit you."

Others said: rather, it is meant generally, for everyone who has this attribute, and no other particular intention is meant.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu Asim narrated to us, he said: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God: ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: "It is not specific to anyone."

The correct view on this matter is that it should be said: God has spoken generally of every scorner and mocker, everyone who has the attribute by which this described one was described, whose path is his path, whoever he may be among people.

* *

His saying: ﴿who has gathered wealth and counted it﴾

He says: the one who gathered wealth and counted its number, and did not spend it in the way of God, nor paid God's right in it, but gathered it, stored it up and kept it.

The readers differed in reading this. Abu Ja'far from the readers of Medina, and the majority of the readers of Kufa except Asim, read "jamma'a" (with emphasis). The majority of the readers of Medina and the Hijaz, except Abu Ja'far, and the majority of the readers of Basra, and Asim from Kufa, read "jama'a" (without emphasis). All of them agree on the emphasis of the dal in ﴿wa 'addadahu﴾ in the sense that I have mentioned in its interpretation. It has been reported from some of the early scholars, through an unsound chain, that he read: "jama'a malan wa 'adadahu" with a light dal, meaning: he gathered wealth and gathered his clan and his numbers. This is a reading I do not consider permissible to recite, since it contradicts the readings of the regions and departs from what the community has agreed upon.

As for His saying ﴿jama'a malan﴾, both the emphatic and the non-emphatic forms are correct in it, since they are two well-known readings in the regional readings, close in meaning; whichever of them the reader recites is correct.

* *

His saying: ﴿He thinks his wealth will make him immortal﴾

He says: he thinks that his wealth, which he gathered and counted, and which he withheld from spending, will make him immortal in this world, averting death from him. It has been said: "akhladahu" means "yukhlidahu" (will make him immortal), as one says of a man who engages in an action that is the cause of his destruction: "So-and-so has perished by God, so-and-so has been ruined by God," meaning that he is ruined by doing that deed, though he has not yet perished nor been destroyed; and like a man who commits a grave sin: "So-and-so has entered the Fire by God."

* *

His saying: ﴿Nay!﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: it is not as he supposed; his wealth does not make him immortal.

Then He informed, may His praise be exalted, that he will be destroyed and punished for his deeds and sins that he used to commit in this world, so He said: ﴿He will surely be thrown into the Crushing﴾. He says: he will surely be hurled into the Crushing on the Day of Resurrection. "Al-Hutama" is one of the names of the Fire, just as it is called Jahannam, Saqar and Laza. I think it was named so because it crushes everything cast into it, just as a greedy man is called "al-hutama." It is reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that he used to read it: "layunbadhanna fi al-Hutama," meaning: this scorner and mocker and his wealth, and so he made it dual for that reason.

* *

His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Crushing is?﴾

He says: and what made you aware, O Muhammad, of what the Crushing is? Then He informed him what it is, saying, may His praise be exalted: it is ﴿the Fire of God, kindled, which rises over the hearts﴾. He says: whose pain and blaze reach the hearts. "Al-Ittila'" (rising over) and "al-buluugh" (reaching) may have the same meaning; it is related from the Arabs by report: "When did our land rise (tala'at)?" and "my land rose (talaat)": meaning it reached.

* *

His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: indeed the Crushing whose description I have given will be closed down upon them, meaning upon these scorners and mockers. ﴿Mu'sada﴾ means: sealed shut. It is recited with both forms (hamz and without hamz), and both have been read.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Talq narrated to us, from Ibn Zuhayr, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿Mu'sada﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Ubayd ibn Asbat narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from Fudayl ibn Marzuq, from Ata', regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Ya'qub narrated to us, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, who said: "In the Fire there is a man in a ravine of its ravines calling for about a thousand years: 'O Hannan! O Hannan!' The Lord of Might says to Jibril: 'Bring out My servant from the Fire.' He comes to it and finds it sealed shut, so he returns and says: 'O Lord, indeed it is closed down upon them.' He says: 'O Jibril, open it and bring My servant out of the Fire.' He opens it, and he comes out like a shadow, and is cast upon the shore of Paradise until God causes hair, flesh and blood to grow for him."

- Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, he said: Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from Mudarris ibn Abd Allah, who said: I heard al-Dahhak ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Locked shut upon them."

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: i.e., sealed shut.

- Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut. The Arabs say: 'awsada al-bab': he closed the door."

* *

His saying: ﴿in extended columns﴾

The readers differed in reading this. The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra recited ﴿fi 'amad﴾ with a fatha on the ayn and the mim. The majority of the readers of Kufa recited "fi 'umud" with a damma on the ayn and the mim. Our view on this is that both are well-known readings, each recited by scholars among the readers, and both are sound dialects. The Arabs pluralize "'amud" (column) as "'umudan" and "'amadan," with both letters vowelled with damma and with fatha; and similarly they do with "ihab" (hide), pluralized as "uhuban" with damma on the alif and the ha', and "ahaban" with fatha on both; and likewise "qadm." Whichever of them the reader recites is correct.

The people of interpretation differed on the meaning of this. Some said: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them in extended columns﴾ means: sealed shut and closed over them; and so it is in the reading of Abdullah, as it has reached us.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Qatada, regarding the reading of Abdullah: "Indeed, it will be closed down upon them in extended columns."

Others said: rather, the meaning is: they will be made to enter into columns, then those columns will be extended over them with pillars.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿in extended columns﴾: he said: "He will make them enter into columns, and they will be extended over them with pillars, and there will be chains around their necks, and the doors will be sealed shut with them."

- Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding ﴿in columns﴾: "of iron, they being bound in them, and those columns are of fire that have been heated by the fire, so they are of fire, extended over them."

Others said: they are columns in which they are tortured.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada regarding ﴿in extended columns﴾: "We used to be told that they are columns with which they are tortured in the Fire." Bishr said: Yazid said: in the reading of Qatada: "'amadin."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada regarding ﴿in extended columns﴾: he said: "A pillar with which they are tortured in the Fire."

The most correct of the sayings on this matter is the saying of the one who said: its meaning is that they will be tortured with columns in the Fire; and God knows best how He tortures them with them. No report has reached us that establishes the manner of their torment with them, nor has He placed for us any indication by which we might grasp the nature of that, so there is no statement on it other than what we have said, which is sound to us; and God knows best.

End of the commentary on Surat al-Humaza.

His saying: ﴿in extended columns﴾

Our view on this is that both are well-known readings, each recited by scholars among the readers, and both are sound dialects. Others said: rather, the meaning is: they will be made to enter into columns, then those columns will be extended over them with pillars.

Mention of those who said that:

Others said: they are columns in which they are tortured.

Mention of those who said that:

All of them agree on the emphasis of the dal in ﴿wa 'addadahu﴾ in the sense that I have mentioned in its interpretation. Mention of those who said that:

- Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding ﴿in columns﴾: "of iron, they being bound in them, and those columns are of fire that have been heated by the fire, so they are of fire, extended over them."

Others said: they are columns in which they are tortured.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada regarding ﴿in extended columns﴾: "We used to be told that they are columns with which they are tortured in the Fire." Bishr said: Yazid said: in the reading of Qatada: "'amadin."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada regarding ﴿in extended columns﴾: he said: "A pillar with which they are tortured in the Fire."

The most correct of the sayings on this matter is the saying of the one who said: its meaning is that they will be tortured with columns in the Fire; and God knows best how He tortures them with them. No report has reached us that establishes the manner of their torment with them, nor has He placed for us any indication by which we might grasp the nature of that, so there is no statement on it other than what we have said, which is sound to us; and God knows best.

End of the commentary on Surat al-Humaza.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 104, verse 1–9:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted be His praise and sanctified be His names: ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker (1) who has gathered wealth and counted it (2). He thinks his wealth will make him immortal (3). Nay! He will surely be thrown into the Crushing (4). And what will make you know what the Crushing is? (5) It is the Fire of God, kindled (6), which rises over the hearts (7). Indeed, it will be closed down upon them (8) in extended columns (9).﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, means by His saying:

﴿Woe to every scorner﴾: al-Wayl (woe) is a valley that flows with the pus and filth of the people of the Fire.

﴿Every scorner﴾: he says: every one who backbites people, defaming them and hating them, as Ziyad al-A'jam said:

"You show me affection when you meet me, though lying, / And when I am absent, you are the scorner and the mocker."

By "al-lumaza" (the mocker) is meant one who disparages people and slanders them.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Musarrik ibn Aban narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from a man he did not name, from Abu al-Jawza', who said: I said to Ibn Abbas: "Who are those whom God began with woe?" He said: "They are those who go about spreading tale-bearing (namima), who separate loved ones, and who seek out the faults of others."

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from his father, from a man of Basra, from Abu al-Jawza', who said: I said to Ibn Abbas: "Who are those whom God summoned to woe?" Then he mentioned something similar to the report of Musarrik ibn Aban.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: he said: "The hamaza is one who eats the flesh of people, and the lumaza is the slanderer."

It has been transmitted from Mujahid a view opposite to this, namely:

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "The hamaza is the slanderer, and the lumaza is the one who eats the flesh of people."

- Musarrik ibn Aban al-Hatstab narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, he said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

It has also been transmitted from him a view contrary to these two, namely:

- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: Yahya narrated to us, he said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: he said: "One of them is the one who eats the flesh of people, and the other is the slanderer." This indicates that the one who transmitted this hadith had become confused about the interpretation of the two words, which is why the narrators' accounts from him differ as I have mentioned.

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: As for the hamaza, it is eating the flesh of people; and as for the lumaza, it is slandering them.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah, from Qatada, who said: "The hamaza is one who eats the flesh of people; the lumaza is one who slanders them."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Khuthaym, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: he said: "Woe to every slanderer who backbites."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliya, who said: "The hamaza: he scorns him to his face, and the lumaza: from behind his back."

- Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, who said: "He scorns him and mocks him with his tongue and his eye, eats the flesh of people, and slanders them."

- al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "The hamaza is with the hand, and the lumaza is with the tongue."

Others have said on this matter:

- Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding the saying of God: ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: "The hamaza is one who scorns people with his hand and strikes them with his tongue, and the lumaza is one who mocks them with his tongue and disparages them."

There has been difference regarding His saying ﴿Woe to every scorner﴾. Some said: it refers to a specific idolater, and some who said this view said: he is Jamil ibn Amir al-Jumahi.

Others among them said: he is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.

Mention of those who said it refers to a specific idolater:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: he said: "An idolater who used to mock people and scorn them."

- Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu Asim narrated to us, he said: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from a man of al-Raqqa who said: "It was revealed concerning Jamil ibn Amir al-Jumahi."

- al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, regarding His saying ﴿scorner and mocker﴾: "It is not specific to anyone; it was revealed concerning all of the Banu Amir." Warqa' said: "al-Raqashi claimed it."

Some of the scholars of Arabic said: this is of the type where the Arabs mention a general name for a thing while intending a particular one, as when a man says to someone: "I will never visit you," and the other replies: "Everyone who does not visit me, then he is not a visitor," the speaker intending a reply to his companion who said to him: "I will never visit you."

Others said: rather, it is meant generally, for everyone who has this attribute, and no other particular intention is meant.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu Asim narrated to us, he said: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God: ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾: "It is not specific to anyone."

The correct view on this matter is that it should be said: God has spoken generally of every scorner and mocker, everyone who has the attribute by which this described one was described, whose path is his path, whoever he may be among people.

* *

His saying: ﴿who has gathered wealth and counted it﴾

He says: the one who gathered wealth and counted its number, and did not spend it in the way of God, nor paid God's right in it, but gathered it, stored it up and kept it.

The readers differed in reading this. Abu Ja'far from the readers of Medina, and the majority of the readers of Kufa except Asim, read "jamma'a" (with emphasis). The majority of the readers of Medina and the Hijaz, except Abu Ja'far, and the majority of the readers of Basra, and Asim from Kufa, read "jama'a" (without emphasis). All of them agree on the emphasis of the dal in ﴿wa 'addadahu﴾ in the sense that I have mentioned in its interpretation. It has been reported from some of the early scholars, through an unsound chain, that he read: "jama'a malan wa 'adadahu" with a light dal, meaning: he gathered wealth and gathered his clan and his numbers. This is a reading I do not consider permissible to recite, since it contradicts the readings of the regions and departs from what the community has agreed upon.

As for His saying ﴿jama'a malan﴾, both the emphatic and the non-emphatic forms are correct in it, since they are two well-known readings in the regional readings, close in meaning; whichever of them the reader recites is correct.

* *

His saying: ﴿He thinks his wealth will make him immortal﴾

He says: he thinks that his wealth, which he gathered and counted, and which he withheld from spending, will make him immortal in this world, averting death from him. It has been said: "akhladahu" means "yukhlidahu" (will make him immortal), as one says of a man who engages in an action that is the cause of his destruction: "So-and-so has perished by God, so-and-so has been ruined by God," meaning that he is ruined by doing that deed, though he has not yet perished nor been destroyed; and like a man who commits a grave sin: "So-and-so has entered the Fire by God."

* *

His saying: ﴿Nay!﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: it is not as he supposed; his wealth does not make him immortal.

Then He informed, may His praise be exalted, that he will be destroyed and punished for his deeds and sins that he used to commit in this world, so He said: ﴿He will surely be thrown into the Crushing﴾. He says: he will surely be hurled into the Crushing on the Day of Resurrection. "Al-Hutama" is one of the names of the Fire, just as it is called Jahannam, Saqar and Laza. I think it was named so because it crushes everything cast into it, just as a greedy man is called "al-hutama." It is reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that he used to read it: "layunbadhanna fi al-Hutama," meaning: this scorner and mocker and his wealth, and so he made it dual for that reason.

* *

His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Crushing is?﴾

He says: and what made you aware, O Muhammad, of what the Crushing is? Then He informed him what it is, saying, may His praise be exalted: it is ﴿the Fire of God, kindled, which rises over the hearts﴾. He says: whose pain and blaze reach the hearts. "Al-Ittila'" (rising over) and "al-buluugh" (reaching) may have the same meaning; it is related from the Arabs by report: "When did our land rise (tala'at)?" and "my land rose (talaat)": meaning it reached.

* *

His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: indeed the Crushing whose description I have given will be closed down upon them, meaning upon these scorners and mockers. ﴿Mu'sada﴾ means: sealed shut. It is recited with both forms (hamz and without hamz), and both have been read.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Talq narrated to us, from Ibn Zuhayr, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿Mu'sada﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Ubayd ibn Asbat narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from Fudayl ibn Marzuq, from Ata', regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Ya'qub narrated to us, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, who said: "In the Fire there is a man in a ravine of its ravines calling for about a thousand years: 'O Hannan! O Hannan!' The Lord of Might says to Jibril: 'Bring out My servant from the Fire.' He comes to it and finds it sealed shut, so he returns and says: 'O Lord, indeed it is closed down upon them.' He says: 'O Jibril, open it and bring My servant out of the Fire.' He opens it, and he comes out like a shadow, and is cast upon the shore of Paradise until God causes hair, flesh and blood to grow for him."

- Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, he said: Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from Mudarris ibn Abd Allah, who said: I heard al-Dahhak ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut."

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Locked shut upon them."

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: i.e., sealed shut.

- Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them﴾: he said: "Sealed shut. The Arabs say: 'awsada al-bab': he closed the door."

* *

His saying: ﴿in extended columns﴾

The readers differed in reading this. The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra recited ﴿fi 'amad﴾ with a fatha on the ayn and the mim. The majority of the readers of Kufa recited "fi 'umud" with a damma on the ayn and the mim. Our view on this is that both are well-known readings, each recited by scholars among the readers, and both are sound dialects. The Arabs pluralize "'amud" (column) as "'umudan" and "'amadan," with both letters vowelled with damma and with fatha; and similarly they do with "ihab" (hide), pluralized as "uhuban" with damma on the alif and the ha', and "ahaban" with fatha on both; and likewise "qadm." Whichever of them the reader recites is correct.

The people of interpretation differed on the meaning of this. Some said: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed down upon them in extended columns﴾ means: sealed shut and closed over them; and so it is in the reading of Abdullah, as it has reached us.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Qatada, regarding the reading of Abdullah: "Indeed, it will be closed down upon them in extended columns."

Others said: rather, the meaning is: they will be made to enter into columns, then those columns will be extended over them with pillars.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿in extended columns﴾: he said: "He will make them enter into columns, and they will be extended over them with pillars, and there will be chains around their necks, and the doors will be sealed shut with them."

- Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding ﴿in columns﴾: "of iron, they being bound in them, and those columns are of fire that have been heated by the fire, so they are of fire, extended over them."

Others said: they are columns in which they are tortured.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada regarding ﴿in extended columns﴾: "We used to be told that they are columns with which they are tortured in the Fire." Bishr said: Yazid said: in the reading of Qatada: "'amadin."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada regarding ﴿in extended columns﴾: he said: "A pillar with which they are tortured in the Fire."

The most correct of the sayings on this matter is the saying of the one who said: its meaning is that they will be tortured with columns in the Fire; and God knows best how He tortures them with them. No report has reached us that establishes the manner of their torment with them, nor has He placed for us any indication by which we might grasp the nature of that, so there is no statement on it other than what we have said, which is sound to us; and God knows best.

End of the commentary on Surat al-Humaza.
